---
title: "Ranking noisy estimates"
subtitle: "1.3 · a simulated league, after Walters' teaching slides"
description: "Effects of unequal sampling precision on the extreme positions of a ranking."
---

Imprecise estimates can place units near the top or bottom of a ranking even when their true values are less extreme. We rank thirty simulated units by estimate. Units with fewer observations have larger standard errors (SEs). Across samples, the true values stay fixed, letting us compare how often each size group appears at either end.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **First draw.** Of the 10 extreme positions by estimate, small units hold 5, medium units 4 and large units 1 in this
  draw; by true value they hold 3 small, 4 medium and 3 large units.
- **True values.** In the first draw, of the top 10 by estimate, 9 are in the true top 10 (7.45 on average over the
  twenty replays). U19, a small unit with true rank 11, is the first of the bottom five: Sampling error moved it down the ranking.
  U18, a large unit with true rank 30, sits two rows above them: noisier small and medium units fell past it, and its
  own estimate came out above its true value.
- **Twenty replays.** The draw menu brings any replay into the table. On average over the 20 replays, small units hold
  4.35 of the 10 extreme positions and large units 2.00, and the estimates order 83.90 of the 435 pairs the wrong way,
  against 88.12 expected over many draws.
- **Replay 11.** In this replay, small units hold 2 extreme positions, medium units 5 and large units 3. Large units hold as many extreme positions in this ranking as in the ranking by true values. Their average across the replays is lower.
- **Extremes highlighted.** When true values are hidden, the shaded rows do not identify which units have genuinely extreme values. The dashed line marks the truth, 3 small and 3 large units.
  Small units sit above it in most replays; large units sit on or below it.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Real units have unknown true values, so this check is not possible. The firms of Kline, Rose and Walters
(2024), KRW, came with SEs of very different sizes: the race estimates have SEs from .025 to .444 (Section V.B; talk
slides 47–49). Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), doi:10.1257/aer.20230700, and deposit doi:10.3886/E198284V1;
